comparisons.decision: Personal baseline vs one fixed range for everyone
comparisons.plain: A fixed range judges everyone against the average woman. A woman whose normal cycle is 37 days gets flagged every single month, even though nothing is wrong for her (our tests check exactly this case). The personal baseline learns her own normal. Measured: it catches more thyroid-like changes (99% vs 85%) and flags fewer healthy people, but on this simulator the fixed range raises slightly fewer false alarms per cycle (3.36 vs 4.27).
comparisons.caveat: Most simulated women have normal cycles well inside 21 to 35 days, which flatters the fixed range. The advantage of a personal baseline should be larger for women whose normal sits near the edges; we have not measured that subgroup separately yet.

comparisons.plain: A z-score alone reacts to sudden jumps but misses slow creeps (it caught only 36% of anemia-like changes). CUSUM catches slow creeps but reacts later. The hybrid combines both and catches PCOS-like changes in the same cycle they start. But the EWMA chart alone does about as well with fewer false alarms (2.92 vs 4.27) and flags fewer healthy people (20% vs 28%).
comparisons.caveat: On these numbers the EWMA chart is a credible replacement for the hybrid. We are reporting that, and it is an open decision for the team.

comparisons.decision: Neural network (GRU) vs simple statistics for spotting change
comparisons.chosen: Simple statistics (Tier 1); GRU kept as Tier 2 under evaluation
comparisons.plain: Neural networks need lots of examples per person. Each simulated person has only 16 to 30 cycles, so simple statistics that track one person's average beat all three neural networks. GRU, LSTM and CNN were almost identical to each other.
comparisons.caveat: With much longer histories, or real data with richer patterns, a neural network could catch up. The GRU is kept, exported and tested, but it does not raise flags.

comparisons.plain: Eight models scored almost the same on symptoms alone, so the data sets the ceiling, not the model. Random forest is near the top everywhere and is the significant winner in two comparisons. It also shows which symptoms mattered and needs no special hardware. The deep neural network was the weakest, which is typical for small tables of data.
comparisons.caveat: On symptoms alone k-NN was fractionally higher and the difference is not significant; any of the top four would be a defensible choice.

comparisons.decision: Symptoms only vs using lab tests
comparisons.plain: Lab tests make the model better (AUC 0.96 vs 0.89), but anyone who already has those tests has seen a doctor. The point of MyCycle is to nudge people before that step, at home, for free. We accept the lower accuracy and state it.
comparisons.caveat: Symptom-only screening will miss some cases; that is why every flag says consider consulting a doctor, and a quiet result is not an all-clear.

rows: All data pooled on a server
comparisons.plain: Pooling everyone's data gives the best accuracy but puts intimate data on a server. Keeping it on each phone alone is private but weak (AUC 0.74). Federated learning keeps data on the phone and gets 0.88, close to pooling.
comparisons.caveat: Measured with 8 simulated phones on the PCOS dataset, not real phones; real networks add dropouts and delays.

comparisons.plain: FedProx ranked slightly better (AUC 0.89 vs 0.88) but got far fewer answers right at the default cut-off (68% vs 83%). FedPer was weakest. FedAvg is the simplest, most standard method and the best balance here.
comparisons.caveat: One run per setting on a small dataset; FedProx's AUC edge could be real. SCAFFOLD and FedAdam were not run.

comparisons.plain: Without noise, a clever server could learn things about one person from her update. Differential privacy adds noise so that any one person barely changes the result, with a measured budget, epsilon. It costs accuracy, and we show exactly how much.
comparisons.caveat: Secure aggregation and homomorphic encryption are other ways to hide updates; we did not test them. DP gives a bounded leak, never zero.

comparisons.decision: Personalizing the neural network per user
comparisons.chosen: Not used (statistical baseline is already personal)
comparisons.plain: Tuning the model on a user's first 4 cycles made it catch more changes, but it also started crying wolf far more often. Too many false alarms make people ignore flags, so we do not use it.
comparisons.caveat: With more cycles for fine-tuning, or a false-alarm penalty during tuning, this could improve.

comparisons.plain: Only 2 of 541 records had a missing answer, so both methods give the same result. We use the simpler one.
comparisons.caveat: On data with many gaps (real app logs), this choice would matter more and should be re-tested.

comparisons.decision: Indian survey (NFHS-5) vs US survey (NHANES) for anemia and thyroid
rows: Indian women aged 15 to 49, our users
comparisons.plain: Our users are Indian women. A US survey would describe a different population, diet and anemia rate. NFHS-5 is India's own survey with real blood measurements.
comparisons.caveat: We did not run NHANES, so this is a reasoned choice, not a measured comparison.

comparisons.decision: PyTorch + ONNX for the model file
comparisons.plain: We needed one model file that runs inside a web page on the phone. PyTorch exports to ONNX in one step and we verified the exported model gives the same answers.
comparisons.caveat: Phone speed and memory have not been measured yet; that benchmark is in progress.
